verses.text: Beloved, don’t believe every spirit, but test the spirits, whether they are of God, because many false prophets have gone out into the world.
By this you know the Spirit of God: every spirit who confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is of God,

and every spirit who doesn’t confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is not of God, and this is the spirit of the Antichrist, of whom you have heard that it comes. Now it is in the world already.
You are of God, little children, and have overcome them; because greater is he who is in you than he who is in the world.
They are of the world. Therefore they speak of the world, and the world hears them.
We are of God. He who knows God listens to us. He who is not of God doesn’t listen to us. By this we know the spirit of truth, and the spirit of error.
Beloved, let us love one another, for love is of God; and everyone who loves has been born of God, and knows God.
He who doesn’t love doesn’t know God, for God is love.
By this God’s love was revealed in us, that God has sent his one and only Son into the world that we might live through him.
In this is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us, and sent his Son as the atoning sacrifice  for our sins.
Beloved, if God loved us in this way, we also ought to love one another.
No one has seen God at any time. If we love one another, God remains in us, and his love has been perfected in us.
By this we know that we remain in him and he in us, because he has given us of his Spirit.
We have seen and testify that the Father has sent the Son as the Savior of the world.
Whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God remains in him, and he in God.
We know and have believed the love which God has for us. God is love, and he who remains in love remains in God, and God remains in him.
In this love has been made perfect among us, that we may have boldness in the day of judgment, because as he is, even so are we in this world.
There is no fear in love; but perfect love casts out fear, because fear has punishment. He who fears is not made perfect in love.
We love him, because he first loved us.
If a man says, “I love God,” and hates his brother, he is a liar; for he who doesn’t love his brother whom he has seen, how can he love God whom he has not seen?
This commandment we have from him, that he who loves God should also love his brother.

footnotes.content: Even in John's day, false teachers moved among the churches. We're told to discern, to *test* what we hear—not with suspicion, but with love and care. The work of the Spirit produces peace and truth; a restless, divisive word that claims to speak for God deserves a second look.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The heart of John's test: does a teaching hold that the Word truly *became flesh*? That God bent down to wear skin, to suffer, to die? If a voice shy away from the humanity of Jesus or His real death and rising, it doesn't speak the Spirit.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Antichrist spirit doesn't always roar; often it whispers a subtle denial—that Christ wasn't truly human, or that His work didn't matter, or that we outgrow the need for Him. Even in John's own time this was already abroad. We feel its echo today.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Little children"—John's term of endearment. He means us. And he's saying: you have already won. Not because you're strong, but because you belong to the One who is. The greater One within you has already overcome all that's set against Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Those who spring from the world speak its language—power, wealth, comfort, self. And the world listens, because it recognizes itself. But we're not of the world; we needn't be alarmed when the world's wisdom rejects us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: John draws a stark line: knowing God is *listening*. The one who knows the Shepherd recognizes His voice. This is how we discern truth from error—not by cleverness alone, but by an ear formed by knowing God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Here John pivots from testing spirits to love. He says love isn't ours to invent—it comes *from* God. Every act of genuine love, every patience, every forgiveness, carries the watermark of the One in whom love began.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "God *is* love." Not that God does love; God is love itself. And therefore if we close ourselves to love—if we harden against another—we're stepping outside of God. This is why John says a loveless person has never known Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God sent His one and only Son—His singular, irreplaceable beloved—into a world that would wound Him. In that one gift we see what love does. It gives up what it prizes most, for those who cannot earn it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: John doesn't say God loved us *because* we were loveable. We loved Him only after He loved us first. He sent His Son to take the weight of our sins—not to punish us, but to reconcile. That upending of the order is the whole Gospel.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If God has loved us with that kind of love—pouring it out at His own cost—then the burden is on us. We haven't earned rest; we've been called to pour it out on one another. This is the answer to false theology: *live like this*.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: No one has ever seen God with their eyes. But when we love one another, we make the invisible visible. We become His hand, His face, His heart to each other. That's how His love completes itself—through us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: We *know* we remain in Him—not by emotion, but by the gift of His Spirit in us. The Spirit is the seal, the evidence, the continual breath. When we feel far from God, this truth anchors: we're given His Spirit, and He doesn't leave.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: John testifies: we have seen that the Father sent the Son to save the world. Not to judge it, not to destroy it—to *save* it. That's the errand. Every time we preach or live the Gospel, we're echoing this: God is on a rescue mission.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: To confess Jesus as the Son of God isn't a password; it's an anchor. It plants you in the love of the Father. He remains in you, and you in Him—a mutual dwelling, a home.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: John repeats: God is love. We've known it, believed it, and now we rest in it. To remain in love is to remain in God; there's no separating them. A life *lived* in love is a life lived in God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Love is made perfect—complete, mature—when we lose our fear of judgment. We can stand boldly because Christ has already stood *for* us. We're clothed in His standing; that's our confidence in the day of reckoning.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Fear and love are opposites—they can't dwell together in the same heart. Fear says, "You'll be punished." Perfect love says, "You're held. You're safe." When we've truly grasped God's love for us, that old terror has nowhere left to hide.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in this simplicity: we don't begin loving. He does. Our love is always *response*, always gratitude for having been loved first. Every gesture of kindness we offer is an echo of the love that reached us long before we reached back.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: John cuts through all pretense: if we claim to love an invisible God but treat a visible brother with cruelty or indifference, we're liars. The proof of our love for God isn't in words—it's in what we do for those we can see.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Here's the commandment: if you love God—and you say you do—then love your brother. Not eventually, not when it's convenient, not when they deserve it. Now. Always. This is the sum of the law and the prophets.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
